Ravana's Council

Stories from the Ramayana

Ravana's Council

When everyone said yes — and one old minister spoke the truth

In everyday English — Yuddha Kanda, sargas 6–16 and 35–36

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it aloud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home.

This book is the story of a council. There is no battle in it — only words. But these words decide what happens next. Where someone flatters, let your voice flatter; where Vibhishana speaks the truth, keep your voice calm and steady; where Ravana grows angry, make your voice heavy.

The yellow boxes hold the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little as you read them — Prahasta proud, Vibhishana humble, Indrajit boastful, Malyavan old and slow.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sargas 6–16 — Ravana's council. Malyavan's counsel came much later — sargas 35–36 — and is told in the last part of this book, on its own. Anything else you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Ravana — king of Lanka, tall and splendid, dark-complexioned, black moustache, tall golden crown, royal robes. A single-headed royal form — as fixed in this series' Ravana book. He will not return Sita.

Prahasta — Ravana's general and greatest minister. Skilled in war, proud, always agreeing with Ravana.

Mahaparshva — Ravana's minister, Mahodara's companion. He too tells Ravana only what Ravana wants to hear.

Indrajit — Ravana's son, also called Meghanada. Master of illusory warfare, very proud of his power.

Vibhishana — Ravana's younger brother. A man of dharma, calm and truthful. He alone speaks the truth in the council.

Malyavan — Lanka's oldest minister, Mandodari's father. Very experienced, calm by nature — he advises Ravana to make peace.

Rama — son of Dasharatha, tall and calm, warm dark-brown skin, bow in hand. He does not appear in person in this book — but the whole council is about him.

1 · The News in Lanka · · THE NEWS IN LANKA

Lanka was burning — Hanuman had set it on fire and gone back across the sea. In Ravana's palace there was silence.

Ravana sat on his throne — and one question circled in his mind — what now? Rama would come — that was certain. Sita was in the Ashoka grove — that too was certain. But Ravana did not want to return Sita.

Ravana called his ministers — “Call the council. Come, all of you. Advise me.”

The ministers came — Prahasta, Mahaparshva, Mahodara, and other great rakshasas. The assembly hall filled up. They all bowed to Ravana — and took their seats.

Ravana said — (slowly, hiding his worry) “Rama is coming — with an army of vanaras. Hanuman burned Lanka. Now tell me — what should be done?”

Silence fell over the council. Everyone looked at one another.

Pause and think — Why did Ravana call the council? Did he really want advice — or did he only want to hear that he was right? And when a king asks for advice, do ministers speak the truth — or only what the king wants to hear?

2 · The Flatterers Speak · · THE FLATTERERS SPEAK

The ministers spoke first — and they all said the same thing — “Your Majesty, there is no one greater than you. Rama is only a man — you will defeat him.”

One said — “We have defeated the gods — what is one man?” Another said — “Vanaras are playthings — we will crush them.”

Then Prahasta spoke — the general, Ravana's most trusted minister. He said —

Prahasta said: “Your Majesty, what is there to worry about? We will fight — and we will win. You have brought Sita — there is no question of returning her now. Let Rama come — we will defeat him here.”

Mahaparshva agreed — “Prahasta is right. Before your Majesty's power, Rama is nothing.”

Ravana smiled. This was what he wanted to hear. Everyone in the council was happy — they all praised Ravana, and Ravana listened to all their praise.

But in one corner of the council sat Vibhishana — silent, grave, head bowed. He was not smiling.

Pause and think — Why were all the ministers saying the same thing? Did they really believe it — or did they want to please Ravana? And when everyone says the same thing, does that make it true?

3 · Vibhishana's Counsel · · VIBHISHANA'S COUNSEL

When everyone fell silent, Vibhishana stood up. Silence fell over the council again — because everyone knew Vibhishana would not say what the others had said.

Vibhishana folded his hands — and said in a calm voice —

Vibhishana said: “Your Majesty, I am your younger brother — and I wish you well. So I speak the truth — return Sita. Make peace with Rama. That is dharma — and that is the protection of Lanka.”

“Rama is no ordinary man. He has killed Khara and Dushana, he has killed Viradha — and he alone can face our whole army. Returning Sita is not defeat — it is wisdom.”

“If we fight, Lanka will burn, our brothers will die, our sons will die — and in the end we too will lose. Your Majesty, there is still time — return Sita.”

The silence in the council grew deeper. No one said anything. Ravana's brows knitted — but he stayed silent.

Vibhishana said again — (slowly, in a steady voice) “I speak the truth, Your Majesty — because I am your brother.”

Pause and think — Why did Vibhishana say what no one wanted to hear? Is speaking the truth also a kind of service? And when everyone is saying yes, how hard is it to stand alone and say no?

4 · The Assembly Meets Again · · THE ASSEMBLY MEETS AGAIN

Ravana did not answer Vibhishana. He rose — and left the assembly hall.

But the next day he called the council again. This time he was even graver. He said — “I have heard what Vibhishana said. But now tell me — how will Lanka be defended?”

Ravana called Prahasta — and said — “Prahasta, take charge of Lanka's defence. Ready the army. Post guards at the gates.”

Prahasta bowed — “As you command, Your Majesty.”

In the council the same talk began again — of war, of power, of victory. Vibhishana sat silent — but there was worry in his eyes.

Ravana said — “Rama will come — and we will fight. Sita will not be returned. This is my final decision.”

Pause and think — Why did Ravana call a second council? Was he thinking over Vibhishana's words — or did he only want to fix his own decision firmly? And when someone has already decided, is calling a council only a show?

5 · Prahasta Argues with Vibhishana · · PRAHASTA ARGUES WITH VIBHISHANA

In the second council Prahasta challenged Vibhishana again. He said — “Vibhishana, you are afraid. You praise Rama — but you forget that we are rakshasas. Before our power, Rama is nothing.”

Vibhishana answered calmly — “I am not afraid, Prahasta. I see the truth. Everyone knows what Rama has done. Dharma is greater than power — and dharma is with Rama.”

Prahasta said — “Wars are not won by dharma — they are won by power.”

Vibhishana said — “Wars can be won by power — but kingdoms are not saved by adharma. Return Sita — that is the protection of Lanka.”

Hearing the two of them, everyone in the council fell silent. No one knew who was right — but everyone knew whose words Ravana wanted to hear.

Ravana looked at Prahasta — and smiled. Vibhishana understood — his words would not be heard.

Pause and think — Prahasta said — wars are won by power. Vibhishana said — kingdoms are not saved by adharma. Which of them is right? And when two people argue, should a king listen to both — or only to the one he likes?

6 · Indrajit Boasts · · INDRAJIT BOASTS

Then Indrajit stood up — Ravana's son, Meghanada. He was young, powerful — and very proud of his illusory powers.

He said — “Father, why do you worry? I am here. I have defeated Indra — Rama is only a man. I will capture him alive and bring him before you.”

Vibhishana said — “Son, do not be proud. You do not know Rama. The one who killed Khara cannot be captured alive by you.”

Indrajit laughed and said — “Uncle, you are afraid — I am not afraid. I fight with maya — and no one can defeat maya.”

Hearing his son, Ravana nodded with pride. He trusted his son — and that trust pleased him.

Vibhishana bowed his head. He understood — in this council there was no place for the truth.

Pause and think — Indrajit said — I will bring Rama back alive. Was that courage — or pride? And when a young man is proud of his power, should the elders stop him — or let him try?

7 · Vibhishana Leaves · · VIBHISHANA LEAVES

In the end Ravana grew angry. He looked at Vibhishana — and said — “You are my brother, yet you praise the enemy! You speak for Rama — then go, go to Rama himself!”

In anger Ravana pushed Vibhishana away — and said — “I do not want your advice. Leave Lanka!”

Silence fell over the council. No one said anything — no one came forward to stop Ravana.

Vibhishana folded his hands — and said in a calm voice — “Your Majesty, I wished you well — that is why I spoke the truth. Now I go — and I will stay where dharma is.”

Vibhishana left Lanka — with his four companions. They walked towards the sea — where Rama's army was.

Ravana was left alone in the council — with his flattering ministers. He felt he had won — but he had lost his truest brother.

Pause and think — Why did Vibhishana leave Lanka? Was he running away from Ravana — or walking towards dharma? And when the one who speaks the truth leaves, does only the yes-sayers remain in the council?

8 · Old Malyavan's Counsel — Later · · OLD MALYAVAN'S COUNSEL — LATER

This part comes much later. After Vibhishana had left, when Rama's army had crossed the sea and come near Lanka, Lanka's oldest minister, Malyavan, spoke to Ravana.

Malyavan was Mandodari's father — and Lanka's most experienced minister. He said to Ravana —

Malyavan said: “Your Majesty, I am old — and I have seen much. Rama is no ordinary man. He is with dharma — and the gods are with him too. Return Sita — and make peace with Rama. That is the protection of Lanka.”

“I say this because I wish you well. If there is war, Lanka will not survive. Your Majesty, peace is the greatest victory.”

Ravana heard Malyavan — and grew angry. He said — “You have grown old — and you are afraid. You too praise Rama! I will not return Sita — and I will defeat Rama here.”

Malyavan blessed Ravana — and went home. He had spoken the truth — but Ravana did not listen.

Then Ravana prepared Lanka's defence — Prahasta at the eastern gate, Mahaparshva and Mahodara at the southern gate, Indrajit at the western gate, Shuka and Sarana at the northern gate, and Virupaksha in the centre of the city. Ravana said — “I myself will go to the northern gate.”

So ended Ravana's council — the truth spoken twice, and twice unheard.

Pause and think — Malyavan said the same thing Vibhishana had said — but much later. Does the truth sometimes need to be said again and again? And when an old, experienced man speaks of peace, should he be heard — or silenced too?

Bigger Thoughts · · BIGGER THOUGHTS

In this book Ravana called a council — but he heard only what he wanted to hear. Prahasta, Mahaparshva and Indrajit praised him — and Ravana was pleased.

Vibhishana spoke the truth — return Sita. Malyavan too spoke the truth — make peace. Ravana heard neither of them. One had to leave Lanka — the other had to go home in silence.

Ask your listeners:

1. Why did Ravana call the council — for advice, or to fix his own decision firmly?

2. When everyone is saying yes, how hard is it to stand alone and speak the truth?

3. Prahasta said — wars are won by power. Vibhishana said — kingdoms are not saved by adharma. Who is right?

4. Indrajit said — I will bring Rama back alive. Was that courage — or pride?

5. Why did Vibhishana leave Lanka — was he running away, or walking towards dharma?

6. Malyavan said the same thing Vibhishana had said — but much later. Does the truth need to be said again and again?

7. If you were in Ravana's place, whose words would you listen to — Prahasta's, or Vibhishana's?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sargas 6–16 and 35–36 — Ravana's council and Malyavan's counsel for peace.

The Council Is Called — Sarga 6

After Hanuman burns Lanka and returns, Ravana calls his ministers together and holds a council — this is sarga 6.

The Flattering Ministers — Sargas 7–8

The ministers praise Ravana and urge him to war; Prahasta speaks — this is sargas 7–8.

Vibhishana's Counsel — Sargas 9–10

Vibhishana advises returning Sita and making peace with Rama — this is sargas 9–10.

The Second Assembly — Sargas 11–12

Ravana calls the assembly again and entrusts Lanka's defence to Prahasta — this is sargas 11–12.

The Arguments — Sargas 14–15

The dispute between Prahasta and Vibhishana, then the dispute between Indrajit and Vibhishana — this is sargas 14–15.

Vibhishana Leaves — Sargas 16–17

Ravana pushes Vibhishana away and drives him out of Lanka; Vibhishana leaves with four companions — Anala, Panasa, Sampati and Prabhasa — this is sargas 16–17.

Malyavan's Counsel — Sargas 35–36, Much Later

Malyavan's counsel for peace is sarga 35 and Ravana's abuse of him is sarga 36 — this happened much after Vibhishana had left, when Rama's army had already crossed the sea. That is why this book tells it in the last part, as a separate chapter — it did not happen in the same sitting as the council. The posting of the guards at the four gates — Prahasta in the east, Mahaparshva and Mahodara in the south, Indrajit in the west, Shuka and Sarana in the north, Virupaksha in the centre — is also sarga 36.

What Happens Next

Vibhishana takes refuge with Rama — and Shuka and Sarana come as spies into Rama's army. Their story is in the next book of this series.

The End · · THE END

Here ends the story of Ravana's council — a council in which everyone said yes — and two men spoke the truth.

And whenever you feel that everyone is saying the same thing, remember Vibhishana — who spoke the truth alone. And whenever an old, experienced man speaks of peace, remember Malyavan — who said that peace is the greatest victory.

— The End —
